conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you during this stay. You’re here because your kidney function has worsened again. Can you tell me how you’ve been feeling since your last discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been a bit dizzy the past few days. My diarrhea has gotten better, but I don’t have much energy. I’m not drinking as much water as before—maybe two bottles a day now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your labs show your creatinine is up to 3.0, which is higher than your baseline. We think this is mostly due to dehydration from not drinking enough and the recent diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. But I still have swelling in my legs. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the swelling is likely from your heart and liver history. An echo showed some tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary hypertension. We’re not restarting your Lasix right now because your kidneys need to stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. What about my tremor? It’s been worse lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your tremor could be from the tacrolimus, which you take for your liver transplant. Your level was a bit high. We’re going to lower the dose to see if that helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. We’re aiming for a safe level that prevents rejection but reduces side effects. Your liver enzymes are a little high, but they’ve been stable and are slowly improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been feeling off-balance, like I might fall to the left.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We think the metronidazole you’re taking for C. diff might be causing that. It can affect balance in some people. We’re going to stop it and keep you on vancomycin only.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know that could happen. Will I still be treated for the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, vancomycin is very effective for C. diff. You’ll finish the full 14-day course. We’re stopping metronidazole because you’re improving and to help with your dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my stomach? I’ve been on omeprazole for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to ranitidine. Omeprazole can sometimes affect the kidneys, especially in people with your history. This change may help your kidney recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take that. When will I start feeling better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You should start feeling more like yourself in a few days. We’re giving IV fluids to help your kidneys, and we’ll keep monitoring your labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning show your creatinine is already down to 2.4. That’s a good sign the fluids are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! And I feel a little less dizzy today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely because we stopped the metronidazole. We also did an ultrasound of your kidneys yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No blockage or stones, which is good. But there are signs that the artery to your right kidney might be narrowed. It’s something to follow up with a kidney specialist after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my kidney function long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could, which is why we want to monitor it. But your other kidney is working well, and we’re already seeing improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. What about my liver? I worry about rejection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked an ultrasound of your liver too. The blood vessels are open, and there’s no sign of blockage. Your enzymes are slowly coming down, so we don’t think it’s rejection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it the hepatitis C again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be, but we’re not certain. We’ll keep an eye on it with your liver doctor. For now, the trend is positive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Completely understandable. We’re also arranging a home safety evaluation. Your team is concerned you might need extra help at home to prevent future hospitalizations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I could use some help with meals and reminders to drink water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we’re setting up. A visiting nurse will check in and help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. Your creatinine is now 1.7, which is close to your baseline. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What changes will I have in my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve lowered your tacrolimus to 1 mg twice a day. You’re now on ranitidine instead of omeprazole. And you’ve stopped metronidazole but will continue vancomycin at home to finish the course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Myfortic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping it stopped for now because of the active infection. Your transplant team will decide when to restart it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to see nephrology for your kidney artery finding and protein in the urine. Also, cardiology for your heart valve and swelling. And your liver doctor to monitor your enzymes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to go. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep drinking fluids, take your meds as directed, and call if you feel dizzy or unwell. We’ll get you set up with home services too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll have your discharge papers ready soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I restart my Lasix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Your heart and kidney doctors will decide that. For now, we’re focusing on keeping your kidney function stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. The nurse will be in shortly with your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for them.
